Results

Do self-report depression and anxiety measures behave similarly across racial groups?

To ensure that any group differences we observed were not driven by the questionnaires themselves, we tested the PHQ-8 and GAD-7 for measurement invariance across racial/ethnic groups using multi-group confirmatory factor analysis (MGCFA). Both scales showed full scalar invariance (PHQ-8: ΔCFI = .0003; GAD-7: ΔCFI = .0004; see Table S1), meaning that we can compare symptoms, and their relationship to language, across groups without differences in questionnaire function as a possible alternative explanation.

We next tested whether racial groups differed in the severity of their internalizing symptoms. A one-way ANOVA indicated that internalizing symptoms differed across racial groups (F(3, 1681) = 5.52, p < .001, ηp² = .01). Specifically, Latino/Hispanic participants reported significantly higher symptoms than Black participants (p Tukey < .001) with no other groups showing significant pairwise differences (M White = 13.2, M Black = 11.4, M Asian = 12.6, M Latino/Hispanic = 14.5, see Table S2 for pairwise comparison). We conducted supplemental robustness checks using entropy balancing 39 via the WeightIt R package 40 to ensure differences in severity across groups did not drive language results. Indeed, primary race-language interactions noted below remained even after reweighting samples so that symptom severity was balanced across groups without needing to subsample or discard participants' data (see Tables S3-S4 for full statistics and SI for full details of these robustness checks).

Do common linguistic markers of psychopathology perform differently across racial groups?

We tested whether key linguistic markers of internalizing symptoms identified in prior work (i.e., I-usage, and positive and negative sentiment) differed in their associations with symptoms across racial/ethnic groups. Linguistic markers were computed using Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC 41 ), a program that calculates the percentage of words in a text belonging to predefined psychological and linguistic categories (i.e., dictionaries). LIWC indexes sentiment through its positive tone and negative tone categories; we thus refer to these variable names when describing them in our analyses, and we use "sentiment" to refer to prior work. For each marker, we estimated an ordinary least squares (OLS) regression model predicting baseline internalizing symptoms from each linguistic feature, race/ethnicity, and their interaction. We also included demographic covariates (age, sex assigned at birth, and education level) in these models. Language × race/ethnicity interaction terms were evaluated with an ANOVA using Type-III sums of squares. Whenever this interaction was significant, we examined group-specific simple slopes and FDR-corrected slope contrasts (i.e., pairwise comparisons). All analyses in the results section focus on contemporaneous associations between baseline language and baseline symptoms, except for the final section, which discusses prediction of follow-up symptom measures.

I-usage.

A significant I-usage × race/ethnicity interaction emerged (F(3, 1662) = 3.48, p = .015), indicating that this association differed across groups. Replicating prior work, I-usage significantly predicted internalizing symptoms among White participants (β = 0.124, 95% CI [0.037, 0.211], p FDR = .021), controlling for age, sex, and education. However, I-usage was not a significant predictor of internalizing symptoms for any racial minority group (i.e., Black, Asian, Latino participants; p FDR > .05; see Figure 2a; see Table S5 for full statistics). FDR-adjusted pairwise contrasts confirmed that the slope for White participants was significantly steeper than the slopes for Black and Latino/Hispanic participants (p FDR < .05). The contrast for Asian participants was in the same direction but did not survive FDR-correction (p FDR = .079). Slopes did not differ significantly among minority groups (all p FDR > .05; see Table S6 for full contrast statistics). Together, these results indicate that I-usage functions as a marker of internalizing distress specifically among White participants.

Negative Tone.

A significant negative tone × race/ethnicity interaction also emerged (F(3, 1662) = 3.28, p = .020; see Figure 2b), indicating that this association differed across groups. Negative tone significantly predicted internalizing symptoms among White participants (β = 0.451, 95% CI [0.380, 0.522], p FDR < .001), controlling for age, sex, and education. Unlike I-usage, however, negative tone was a significant predictor of internalizing symptoms across all racial/ethnic groups (all p FDR 's < .001; see Table S5 for full statistics). Pairwise contrasts revealed that only the slopes for White and Latino/Hispanic participants differed significantly, such that negative tone carried a stronger association with internalizing symptoms among Latino/Hispanic participants than among White participants (p FDR = .012). No other pairwise contrasts were significant (all p FDR > .05; see Table S6 for full contrast statistics). Together, these results indicate that negative tone tracks internalizing distress across all racial/ethnic groups, but this signal, in our sample, is amplified specifically among Latino/Hispanic participants.

Positive Tone.

Similar to negative tone, a significant positive tone × race/ethnicity interaction was observed (F(3, 1662) = 5.00, p = .002; Figure 2c). Positive tone significantly predicted internalizing symptoms among White participants (β = -0.365, 95% CI [-0.450, -0.280], p FDR < .001; see Figure 2c), such that greater positive tone was associated with fewer internalizing symptoms, controlling for age, sex, and education. Positive tone was also a significant predictor across all racial/ethnic minority groups (all p FDR < .001; see Table S5 for full statistics). Interestingly, none of the White-versus-minority contrasts reached significance after FDR-correction (all p FDR > .05; see Table S6 for full contrast statistics). Instead, significant slope differences emerged among minority groups: Slopes were significantly stronger for Asian than Black participants (p FDR = .004) and for Latino/Hispanic than Black participants (p FDR = .024). The contrast for Asian-Latino/Hispanic participants was not significant (p FDR > .05). Thus, higher positive tone tracks lower internalizing symptoms across all racial/ethnic groups, but this association was significantly weaker among Black participants relative to Asian and Latino/Hispanic participants. Additional language variables. We also examined a subset of other LIWC variables of theoretical interest (social words, we-words, and cognitive processing words) but found that none of these categories significantly interacted with race/ethnicity to track symptoms (p FDR > .2, see Figure S1a-c and Tables S7- S8 for full results). Across groups, internalizing symptoms were associated with greater cognitive processing word usage, but symptoms were not significantly associated with social or we-word usage.

What are the linguistic patterns that characterized internalizing symptoms across and within racial groups?

We next used differential language analysis 42 to identify the words, phrases, and topics that correlated with internalizing symptom severity both across and within racial/ethnic groups. This technique differs from dictionary-based approaches, like LIWC, as it does not restrict analyses to a predefined word list. We conducted two analyses: (1) an n-gram analysis identifying specific words and short phrases whose association with symptom severity varied by group, and (2) topic modeling, testing whether the frequency of semantically coherent language clusters ('topics') showed differential associations with internalizing symptoms across groups.

N-grams.

We identified all 1-to 3-word phrases (i.e., 1-to 3-grams) whose frequency was associated with internalizing symptom severity for each group. This yielded a total of 59 n-grams that were significantly associated with internalizing symptoms within at least one group after FDR-correction and controlling for age, sex at birth, and education-level. We then tested whether n-grams were associated with symptoms in each of our four racial/ethnic groups to identify which linguistic markers of distress were unique or shared across groups (see Figure 3; full statistics are presented in Table S9).

Six (10%) n-grams showed significant associations with internalizing symptoms across all four groups. These shared markers of distress included general psychological and evaluative terms (e.g., "low", "easier", "depressed", "exhausted", "good").

Another 13 (22%) n-grams were significantly associated with internalizing symptoms in two or three racial/ethnic groups, representing common signals of psychopathology that cut across group boundaries. These shared markers spanned both affective and evaluative language. Terms reflecting explicit negative affect and clinical distress ( "sad", "anxious". "anxiety", "depression", and "failure") were shared across multiple groups, as were evaluative terms describing life satisfaction ("dissatisfied", "satisfied", "poor") and general difficulty ("hard", "difficult"). Notably, several shared markers were negatively associated with internalizing symptoms, indicating that use of positively valenced terms such as "happy", "satisfied", and "higher" were associated with less distress across groups.

The remaining 40 n-grams (68%) were significantly associated with symptoms in only a single group, and their semantic content differed substantially across groups. Black participants showed the largest set of group-specific markers (N = 15), featuring somatic and physical language alongside affective terms (e.g., "pain", "weak", "stomach", "angry"). White participants' 14 group-specific markers centered on chronicity and cognitive framing (e.g., "chronic", "never", "hopeless" ). Asian participants' 8 group-specific markers emphasized temporal and mood-tracking language (e.g., "mood_lower_usual", "couple weeks"). Latino/Hispanic participants had the fewest group-specific markers (N = 3, "terrible", "find", "worse").

Topic Modeling.

We then tested whether the use of words within "topics" (i.e., groups of words shown to cluster into semantic themes) showed differential associations with internalizing symptoms across race/ethnicity groups. We selected and tested 54 of 2,000 topics drawn from a pretrained model developed by past researchers 42 . Twenty-two topics showed significant main effects on internalizing symptoms after correction (p FDR < .05), spanning constructs including depression, romantic loss, chronic illness, and physical pain. However, only two topics showed significant interactions with race/ethnicity in predicting internalizing symptoms (p FDR < .05; see Figure 4). First, we observed a significant interaction between race/ethnicity and the presence of the Physical Pain and Bodily Discomfort topic (F(3, 1662) = 6.31, p FDR < .001). Greater use of words in this topic, characterized by musculoskeletal and somatic language (e.g., "neck," "stiff," "muscle," "aches," "shoulder"), significantly predicted internalizing symptoms among White participants (β = 0.064, 95% CI [0.006, 0.122], p FDR = .031; see Table S10), when controlling for age, sex, and education. However, a comparison of slopes indicated that this association was significantly stronger for the three minority groups than for White participants (p FDR < .05; see Table S11 for full statistics). Slopes did not differ significantly among the three minority groups (all p FDR > .05; see Table S11 for full contrast statistics). Together, these results indicate that somatic language carries a stronger signal of internalizing distress among racial/ethnic minority groups than among White participants, consistent with prior work documenting different norms linking somatic symptom expression to psychological disclosures across racial/ethnic groups.

The Depression Symptoms and Negative Affect topic, characterized by words like "gutted," "poorly," "bummer," "depressed," and "disappointed," also showed a significant race/ethnicity interaction (F(3, 1662) = 9.31, p FDR < .001). This topic significantly predicted internalizing symptoms among all groups (p FDR < .01; see Table S10 for full statistics). However, contrasts confirmed the slope for Asian participants was significantly weaker than those observed among White, Black, and Latino/Hispanic participants (p FDR ≤ .001). Slopes did not differ significantly among White, Black, and Latino/Hispanic participants (all p FDR > .05; see Table S11 for full contrast statistics). Thus, this cluster of affective language is a less reliable marker of internalizing severity among Asian participants, which may reflect cultural differences in the directness of emotional expression.

Can machine-learning models predict psychopathology equivalently across groups?

The analyses above relied on word frequency, which do not account for the context in which words are used. Word embeddings resolve this issue by representing text in a high-dimensional space organized around meaning. Machine-learning (i.e., ridge regression) models can learn to predict symptoms based on word embeddings with high accuracy 10 . We next tested whether such approaches could predict internalizing symptoms in our sample and whether these models performed equivalently across racial/ethnic groups.

Within-group performance. We generated contextual word embeddings for each participant's language using MentalRoBERTa, and used these embeddings as features in a ridge regression model to predict internalizing symptoms with 5-fold cross validation. Results showed our model predicted internalizing symptoms from participants' written text with strong accuracy across the full sample (r = 0.738, 95% CI [0.719, 1], p < .001). We next built four group-specific models, each trained and evaluated on text within each racial group using 5-fold cross-validation with a fixed penalty. We found that each model performed well in predicting internalizing symptoms within the same racial group: White (r = 0.708, 95% CI [0.665, 1,] p < .001), Black (r = 0.690, 95% CI [0.657, 1], p < .001), Asian (r = 0.753, 95% CI [0.713, 1], p < .001), and Latino/Hispanic (r = 0.742, 95% CI [0.701, 1], p < .001). In fact, a one-way ANOVA on participant-level absolute prediction errors (i.e., the absolute difference between predicted and self-reported symptom scores) revealed no significant difference across racial/ethnic groups (F(3, 1681) = 2.223, p = .084, ηp² = .004), indicating comparable model performance across groups.

Comparing within-group and across-group predictions. Next, we examined how well models trained on one racial/ethnic group's language data generalized to unseen data from another group by computing the difference in error for across-group predictions vs. that target group's own in-group model (see Figure 5 and Methods for details). We found that the White-trained model produced significantly higher error predicting internalizing symptoms for Black, Latino/Hispanic, and Asian participants than each of those groups' own models produced (p FDR < .001; see Table S12 for full statistics). Minority-trained models showed a more differentiated pattern. The Black-trained model produced significantly higher error for Asian participants than the Asian model did (p FDR = .002). By contrast, the Latino/Hispanic-and Asian-trained models produced significantly lower error on White participants' text than the White model produced on its own group (p FDR 's = .015 and .002 respectively). Across all 12 pairings, the White-trained model was the only one with significantly higher error than the target group's own model for all three other groups. Each minority-trained model, by contrast, showed higher error for zero or one other group.

What do these machine learning models learn differently for each race?

To better understand why the models differed, we examined how each group's model weighted language when estimating symptom severity. Each model learned a vector in embedding space that points from low-to high-severity language. The cosine similarity of these vectors (a measure of how closely two vectors align;1 = identical,0 = unrelated) ranged from 0.796 to 0.891 (see Table S13), indicating that all groups' models learned broadly similar, but not identical, patterns to gauge severity. Interestingly, the three minority groups' severity vectors were more similar to one another (mean pairwise cosine similarity = 0.847) than to the White model's (mean = 0.807). This parallels the results above, in which the White-trained model was the only one with higher error on every other group. Thus, for the word-level analyses that follow, we collapse the three minority-group vectors into a single mean minority-group vector for the primary comparison reported below (see Figure S2 for analyses of each minority model).

We then computed a vector that captures the difference in what the White-model vs. minority-model had learned to associate with symptoms, and we projected words onto this difference vector, which shows how much that word contributes to a given model's severity predictions 43 . Figure 6 shows, for each displayed word, the difference between the two models: how much more strongly one model links that word to high severity than the other does. Words at the extremes are therefore the ones on which the two models disagree most.

This analysis showed that the two models learned to associate different words with internalizing symptoms. Compared to the minority-group model, the White model linked high severity more strongly with agentic, self-focused, and goal-directed language including words like: "myself", "goals", "self", "motivated", "focus", "concentration", and "decision" alongside engagement and interest-related language such as "interest," "hobbies", "enjoy", "reading", and "activities." The minority-group model, by contrast, was dominated by temporal and seasonal language, with "earlier", "holidays", "cold", "lately", "weather", "later", "morning", "early", and "nights" among the words most strongly weighted toward severity. This suggests that whereas the White model's severity direction relied more on self-referential, motivational, and interest-based content, the minority-group model's severity direction relied more on temporal framing, such as references to time of day, recency, and seasonal or holiday context. A secondary pattern also emerged for the minority-group model around describing functional change ("harder", "easier", "better", "different", "bad", "fine"), suggesting relatively greater sensitivity to language describing change relative to a prior baseline. Analyses of each minority racial/ethnic group's model against the White model showed similar patterns to this overall contrast (see Figure S2). severity between the White model and the combined minority models (Black, Asian, Latino/Hispanic averaged together). Positive (teal) values mean the White model links that word more strongly to high severity than the averaged minority-group model; negative (grey) values mean the reverse. The x-axis shows how much more strongly one model weights that word toward severity, with larger absolute values indicating greater disagreement between groups in how strongly that word signals severity. All models were fit with matched hyperparameters (λ = 250) so that differences in the learned weights are not attributable to differences in regularization. The figure shows the 20 words at each end of the distribution of weight differences.

Testing prediction of follow-up symptom measures

We designed this study to allow us to examine whether the ability to predict follow-up symptoms assessed three weeks later based on baseline language (as in Hur et al. 38 ) also differed across races (see Tables S14-16). None of the LIWC variables predicted follow-up symptoms after controlling for baseline symptoms, and none showed moderation by race (see Supplemental Information). These null predictions may be due to the fact that symptoms were highly stable across the three-week period (r = .817, 95% CI [.799, .833], p < .001). Indeed, machine-learning models trained on baseline language also could not significantly predict follow-up symptoms when baseline symptoms were controlled for (all |Δr| ≤ .006, all p FDR ≥ .66; Table S15). These machine-learning models controlling for baseline symptoms also showed no cross-group differences in prediction accuracy (all p FDR ≥ .85; Table S16).

Interestingly, though, machine learning models trained on baseline language did predict follow-up symptoms when baseline symptoms were not controlled for (r pooled = 0.565, 95%CI [0.535, 1], p < .001), and the cross-group asymmetry in predictive accuracy was still present:

The White-trained model again produced significantly higher error for all three minority groups than each group's own model did in predicting follow-up symptoms (Table S14; Figure S3). Thus, racial differences in the accuracy of language-based estimates are not confined to a single timepoint and persist to symptom reports three weeks later, but neither LIWC features nor these machine learning models predicted change in symptoms when baseline symptoms are controlled for.

Discussion

Language-based assessments are increasingly proposed as scalable, low-burden supplements to closed-ended symptom scales, and a growing body of work shows they can index psychological health with remarkable accuracy 16, 44, 45 . However, the utility of these measures rests on an assumption that the associations between language and symptoms are the same regardless of who is producing that language. Here we extend initial evidence challenging this assumption 29 using three complementary language analyses in a large, racially stratified sample of U.S. adults spanning four racial/ethnic groups. We found that first-person singular pronoun use, a well-established marker of depression 21, 22, 25 , predicted internalizing symptoms among White participants but not Black, Asian, or Latino/Hispanic participants. Associations between symptoms and sentiment markers also differed across groups: Negative sentiment was more strongly linked to symptoms for Latino than White participants and positive sentiment was more strongly linked for Latino than Black participants. A differential language analysis recovered a core set of words and phrases that characterized symptoms across all four groups, along with phrases and topics that were group-specific. Interestingly, somatic language carried a stronger signal of distress among minority groups than among White participants. Machine learning models trained within each group predicted symptoms accurately for that group. However, they did not transfer equivalently when deployed out-of-group; the White-trained model produced significantly higher error for all three racial/ethnic minority groups than those groups' own models did. Finally, an interpretive technique linking model predictions back to individual words revealed that the White model weighted self-focused, agentic language more heavily than minority models. These findings suggest language-based tools cannot assume uniform validity and must be evaluated for the populations they serve. Like Rai et al. 29 , we found that I-usage predicted depression severity among White but not Black participants, and that a model trained on White participants' language produced higher error for Black participants than a model trained on Black participants' own language did. Here, we extend this result in several ways. First, we demonstrated that the pattern was not confined to the Black-White comparison, as I-usage also did not predict symptoms among Latino/Hispanic participants or Asian participants. Second, we found that other language markers showed more nuanced patterns of associations with symptoms across groups. Sentiment (i.e., the positivity or negativity of language) predicted internalizing symptoms in all four groups. However, the association for negative sentiment was stronger among Latino/Hispanic than White participants. Thus, it does not appear that language-based assessments perform uniformly across minority groups. Instead, different linguistic features may over or underestimate symptoms, depending on the racial group. Third, we showed that this effect emerges outside of social media platforms. Many prior demonstrations of language features predicting mental illness from language have relied on social media text 14, 28, 29, 46 , raising the possibility that platform-specific disclosure norms 36,37 , rather than differences in expression, could help to explain the observed effects. We fixed the disclosure context across groups by analyzing participants' responses to prompts validated by prior research 38 . This helped minimize concerns about group differences emerging due to norms for how distress is expressed on various platforms. An additional goal was to test whether these group differences in language-symptom associations extend to the prospective prediction of symptom change. LIWC-based markers did not significantly predict follow-up symptoms in any group after controlling for baseline severity, likely because symptoms were highly stable across the three-week assessment window, leaving little residual variance for these features to explain (see Supplemental Information).

We also found that machine learning models did not transfer equally across training and test groups. Across all twelve model-group pairings, the White-trained model was the only one to produce significantly higher error than every other group's own in-group model. By contrast, the Asian-and Latino/Hispanic-trained models each produced significantly lower prediction error for White participants than the White model produced on its own group. This pattern argues against an obvious alternative explanation that minority-group models performed worse because they were trained on less data and were therefore noisier. If that were the case, the minority-trained models, not the White-trained model, should have generalized poorly to other groups. Instead, it seems that the content each model learns to associate with symptoms is more similar for minority-trained models than the White-trained model. Indeed, although the four groups' learned severity directions were broadly similar, with pairwise cosine similarities ranging from .796 to .891, they differed in what words they weighted to be aligned with higher internalizing symptoms. The White model's severity direction was anchored in agentic, self-referential, and motivational content, aligning with cognitive theories of depression 23, 47, 48 . The minority-mean direction was anchored instead in temporal and seasonal framing, alongside language describing functional change relative to a prior baseline. This suggests that the White model weighs some linguistic features differently from those most informative for these groups, which could contribute to its higher cross-group prediction error. This asymmetry also held when models trained on baseline language predicted symptoms three weeks later. However, because symptoms were highly stable, this prospective prediction was eliminated once baseline symptoms were included. Thus, the higher cross-group error persists when predicting symptom scores at a later timepoint (but not when predicting changes in those scores relative to baseline).

Similarly, our differential language analyses showed that somatic and physical language carried a stronger signal of internalizing symptoms among minority groups than among White participants. This pattern emerged both in topic modeling and n-gram analyses where the physical pain topic and phrases like "stomach," "terrible," and "pain" were only associated with symptoms for minority participants. This pattern aligns with prior arguments that Black and Latino/Hispanic groups talk about mental health concerns in terms of somatic issues 30, 33 , though see 49, 50 for contrasting views. Other results were also consistent with past research. In particular, the Depression Symptoms and Negative Affect topic was a weaker marker of symptoms for Asian participants than other groups. This is in line with research that shows individuals of Asian heritage often suppress emotions more than their European-American counterparts, and that the link between suppression and depressive symptoms is attenuated for Asian individuals 51 . As a result, language sentiment may therefore be a weaker indicator of psychological distress for Asian individuals. These findings highlight the power of language-based analyses to uncover relevant psychological constructs and prompt further research on the psychological and linguistic patterns that index pathology in each group 10, 52.

A key question for our findings is whether they reflect actual differences in how distress is expressed across groups or instead artifacts of measurement, sampling, or context. Several aspects of our design allow us to speak against some of the most plausible alternative explanations. First, our mental health measures showed comparable functioning across groups, which reduces the likelihood that differences in language-symptom associations reflect differences in how the symptom measures themselves behaved. Second, although racial/ethnic groups differed in mean baseline symptom severity, effects that paralleled these differences were robust when we equated groups on severity with entropy balancing. Third, as discussed above, scholars have raised the concern that platform-specific disclosure norms 36, 37 , rather than differences in expression, may motivate the observed effects. However, we fixed the disclosure context across groups by analyzing responses to the same prompts validated by prior research 38 , so such norms are unlikely to serve as explanations for our findings. Finally, an overlapping constellation of results emerged across three different analytic approaches: a dictionary-based program 41 , n-gram and topic analyses 42, 53 , and machine learning models trained on word embeddings 54, 55 , suggesting these differences reflect a property of the language-symptom relationship rather than an artifact of any particular method.

Our work has several implications for language-based mental health research. Most importantly, our results caution against treating language-based assessment models as validated once they produce acceptable pooled accuracy benchmarks, a practice that is increasingly common as digital mental health platforms adopt language-based screening at scale 45, 56 . The higher cross-group prediction error we observed suggests that a model trained predominantly on one group's language (as many existing tools often are, given the demographic composition of social media and clinical training corpora) 57, 58 , could systematically under or over-estimate symptom severity for the very populations facing the greatest structural barriers to traditional care. This difference would carry little to no signal in aggregated performance metrics, such that a tool could appear validated while producing less accurate estimates for the populations it most needs to reach. In fact, this presents a critical gap for platforms already deploying language-based screening at scale, echoing the pitfalls of the "one-size-fits-most" approach documented in other clinical algorithms 34 . This concern is not new to psychometrics, as research has documented that both clinical and educational instruments can function differently across demographics, and ignoring these differences can perpetuate structural inequalities 59, 60 . Longer-term, our findings point toward a more targeted solution where model developers audit which specific features drive predictions for a given population and reweight or retrain accordingly. Achieving this kind of targeted, population-sensitive validation is unlikely to happen within a siloed field. It will require sustained collaboration between people like the computer scientists who build these models, clinicians and cultural psychologists who understand how distress is expressed across groups [61] [62] [63] , and more importantly the communities these tools are meant to serve.

Although the use of a large racially stratified sample, validated prompts, and convergence across diverse analytic methods are strengths of the current research, several limitations should be addressed by future work. Most importantly, individual difference measures like race and ethnicity are often coarse measurements of the underlying processes that shape language use, including emotion socialization, cultural context, acculturation, and lived experiences 32, 61, 62, 64 . Although we document variation across these broad social categories, future work should identify the underlying psychological and cultural processes that drive these differences. Our four-group design also collapsed distinctions that are likely to matter, including those across East, South, and Southeast Asian participants. This precludes us from testing differences in acculturation, generational status, or language background. Identifying which processes motivate these differences, such as help-seeking norms 4 , or other social features, requires measuring them directly rather than inferring them from group membership alone. Additionally, our sample was recruited online, resided in the United States, wrote in English, and spanned a largely subclinical to moderate range of symptom severity. This presents a rich open set of questions for future research around whether these patterns hold in clinical populations, in other languages or cultures, and whether illness severity modulates these associations.

Language-based assessments hold considerable promise for expanding access to mental health screening at scale, without the added cost or clinical infrastructure traditional assessment requires. However, to deploy them effectively, we must address the differences in cross-group accuracy that we found here. These findings provide further evidence that the validity of language-based assessments must be established on populations they are intended to serve, rather than assumed from average performance in pooled samples. However, doing so is possible with existing tools, and careful attention to the linguistic signals of distress used by diverse groups can also guide psychological theory and discovery.

Methods

Open Science Statement

All data and analytic code can be accessed at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22877408. Statistical analyses were performed using R Version 4.5.0 65 . This study was not preregistered. Our central hypothesis, that language-symptom associations vary by race/ethnicity, was generated prior to launching the study, inspired by Rai et al. 29 . We extended their methods and analytic approach to four racial/ethnic groups and added two additional methods: n-gram analysis and embedding projections. The specific words, phrases, and topics these methods identified were not preregistered, given that open-vocabulary and embedding-based methods surface patterns from the data rather than testing a predefined list. Lastly, given the number of analyses we report, we applied an FDR-correction 66 within each analysis family (e.g., across a given LIWC variable's pairwise group contrasts, across all candidate n-grams within a group, across all 54 candidate topics, across machine learning model comparisons) to reduce inflated error from multiple comparisons.

Participants

We initially recruited N = 1,798 adults via Prolific Academic between December 2025 and April 2026. Eligibility criteria required current U.S. residency, age between 18 and 65, a minimum of 1,000 prior Prolific submissions, an approval rate of 95% or above, and self-identification as Black/African American, East Asian, South Asian, Southeast Asian, Latino/Hispanic, or White.

An a priori power analysis indicated that a minimum of N = 350 participants per racial/ethnic group would provide 80% power to detect an effect of r = 0.15 (α = .05). Therefore, we targeted 400 participants per group to account for attrition and data quality exclusions, yielding a recruitment goal of a minimum of 1,600 participants. To achieve racial/ethnic stratification, we used Prolific Academic's ethnicity filter to oversample Black/African American, East Asian, South Asian, and Latino/Hispanic participants, supplemented by open recruitment for White participants. Of the 1,798 initially recruited, 113 were excluded from analyses for not completing the survey, either due to missing demographic data (N = 29), or for failing to self-identify within the four target racial/ethnic groups (N = 84). This ultimately produced a final sample of N = 1,685. Demographics by group are reported in Table 2. All procedures were approved by the Princeton University Institutional Review Board (Protocol #17793). Participants provided informed consent prior to enrollment. Participants were compensated $5.00 upon completion of Session 1 (approximately 25 minutes) and $4.00 upon completion of Session 2 (approximately 5 minutes), for a total of $9.00.

Procedure

At Session 1 (baseline), participants completed nine open-ended mental health prompts adapted from Hur et al. 38 (presented in randomized order), followed by the PHQ-8 and GAD-7. To mitigate AI usage in open-ended response questions, copy-paste functionality was disabled for all writing tasks, and a minimum 30-second response window was enforced before participants could advance. Participants whose concatenated responses contained fewer than 25 words were excluded, consistent with standard NLP preprocessing threshold recommendations 67 . Attention checks (e.g., "Select 'Strongly Agree'" and "Copy and paste this text") were embedded throughout to further promote data quality. At Session 2, approximately three weeks later, participants completed the PHQ-8 and GAD-7 again. Figure 1 illustrates the data collection timeline. Using LIWC variables, we found no significant prospective associations between baseline language and follow-up symptoms after controlling for baseline symptom severity. Accordingly, all LIWC results reported in the main text reflect contemporaneous associations between language and symptoms; we report the prospective LIWC analyses in the Supplemental Information. Machine learning models significantly predicted follow-up symptoms when baseline symptoms were not included, but not after controlling for baseline symptoms. We summarize these results in the main text and report full statistics in the Supplemental Information.

Materials

Open-Ended Mental Health Prompts. At the baseline session, participants provided diary-style written responses to nine open-ended questions about their recent mental health experiences (e.g., "How has your energy been over the last two weeks?" ; adapted from prior work 38 ) and presented in randomized order. Prompts were designed to map onto core symptom domains of depression and anxiety (see Table 1 for full prompt list). Responses across all nine prompts were concatenated into a single text per participant, which was used for all language analyses. Self-Report Measures. Depressive symptom severity was assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire-8 (PHQ-8) 68 , and generalized anxiety symptom severity was assessed using the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) 69 . Both scales demonstrated excellent internal consistency in our sample, with reliability consistent across racial/ethnic groups: PHQ-8: α = .915 overall (Asian = .920, Black = .909, Latino/Hispanic = .918, White = .914); GAD-7: α = .937 overall (Asian = .941, Black = .933, Latino/Hispanic = .941, White = .932). PHQ-8 and GAD-7 baseline scores were highly correlated (r = 0.84, 95% CI [0.83, 0.86], p < .001), consistent with the high comorbidity of depression and anxiety and the shared internalizing factor structure 70 . Accordingly, as in prior work [16] [17] [18] [19] , we computed an internalizing composite by summing PHQ-8 and GAD-7 scores (range: 0-45), which served as the primary outcome for all analyses.

Analytic Strategy

Do self-report depression and anxiety measures behave similarly across racial groups? Before comparing PHQ-8 and GAD-7 scores across racial/ethnic groups, we first verified that both scales measured depression and anxiety similarly across groups, a prerequisite for valid group comparisons. If a scale functions differently across groups (e.g., if the same response reflects different levels of distress for different people), then observed score differences could reflect measurement artifacts rather than true differences in symptoms. We tested this using MGCFA, a statistical approach that examines whether a questionnaire's underlying structure holds equally across groups 71 . We tested three levels of equivalence in sequence. First, we asked whether the same items cluster together into the same factor across groups (configural invariance). Second, we asked whether each item was equally strongly related to the underlying construct across groups (metric invariance). Third, we asked whether participants from different groups who endorse the same level of symptoms tend to select the same response options (scalar invariance). Models were estimated using methods appropriate for ordinal response scales (DWLS estimator), and we used White participants as the reference group. Invariance at each level was supported when model fit did not meaningfully worsen upon adding constraints (ΔCFI < .010, ΔRMSEA < .015) 72 . Please see Table S1 for full results.

Do common linguistic markers of psychopathology perform differently across racial groups?

To test whether the association between specific word classes and internalizing symptoms differed across racial/ethnic groups, we quantified six psycholinguistic variables using LIWC-22 41 : first-person singular pronoun use (I-usage), negative sentiment (negative tone), positive sentiment (positive tone), first-person plural pronoun use (we-words), social language, and cognitive processing words. I-usage, negative sentiment, and positive sentiment were the primary predictors of interest given prior evidence that all three vary across racial/ethnic groups and relate to internalizing symptoms 22, 25, 29 . The remaining variables were examined as secondary analyses. To test whether race/ethnicity moderated these associations, we estimated OLS regression models predicting baseline internalizing symptoms from each language feature, race/ethnicity, their interaction, and demographic covariates (age, sex at birth, education). All continuous variables were standardized prior to modeling, and race/ethnicity was dummy-coded with White as the reference group. Whenever this interaction was significant, we examined group-specific simple slopes and FDR-corrected 66 slope contrasts using the emtrends function from the emmeans package 73.

What linguistic patterns are associated with psychopathology across and within racial groups? N-grams. We extracted 1-3 word sequences (n-grams) from each group's responses using the topicsGrams function from the topics package in R 53 . In line with prior work 67, 74 , we applied three standard filters: n-grams had to 1) appear in at least 1% of responses, 2) have a pointwise mutual information (PMI) score > 3, and 3) fall within the top 5,000 n-grams per group. These filters ensure that retained n-grams were both common and linguistically coherent in our corpus. Within each group, we built OLS regression models via the topicsTest function, regressing standardized internalizing symptoms onto each standardized n-gram usage frequency while controlling for demographic covariates. We controlled for multiple comparisons using FDR-correction 66 within each racial/ethnic group. The extracted words and phrases were then classified into three groups: universal (significant associations in all four groups), shared (significant associations in two to three groups), or group-specific (significant associations in exactly one group). For n-grams significant in more than one group, effect sizes were pooled using Fisher's z-transformation 75.

Topic modeling.

We applied a pre-trained 2,000-topic Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) model trained on Facebook status updates 42 , to assign each participant a probability score per topic (i.e., a cluster of words that reflect a semantic focus, like "shopping" or "parents") using the Differential Language Analysis ToolKit 76 . To restrict the number of tests we conducted (and avoid inflated error levels from testing 2,000 topics), we performed a multi-stage filtering process to exclude topics likely to be irrelevant to our research question. First, we passed the list of words within each topic through LIWC and computed for each a composite score averaging standardized loadings across 28 relevant affective and social LIWC categories (e.g., negative emotion, anxiety, social behavior, health, etc.). We excluded topics whose scores fell in the bottom 75% of these scores, leading to 500 topics that fell in the top quartile of affective and psychological language content. Second, the first author manually reviewed this set and retained topics corresponding to clinically relevant constructs (e.g., emotional exhaustion, hopelessness, anhedonia, rumination, somatic symptoms, suicidality, panic, sleep disturbance, self-esteem, trauma). Third, to ensure that we had not missed relevant topics in our first exclusion process, the first author re-reviewed all 2,000 topics and selected 32 additional topics that appeared to be relevant. This resulted in a final candidate set of 54 topics. For each of these 54 topics, we estimated OLS models predicting internalizing symptoms from topic usage, race/ethnicity, and their interaction; 2 topics survived FDR correction (p FDR < .05) and were carried forward for group-specific slope estimation and pairwise contrasts via emtrends and emmeans.

Can machine-learning models predict psychopathology equivalently across groups?

Word embeddings. To test whether machine learning models trained on open-ended language could predict internalizing symptoms, and critically whether predictive accuracy differed across racial/ethnic groups, we generated contextual word embeddings using MentalRoBERTa-base 54 , a 12-layer transformer language model fine-tuned on mental health text. Embeddings were extracted using the textEmbed function from the Text package in R 55 . Following prior work 11, 44, 77 , we extracted the penultimate layer (11th layer) and mean-pooled across tokens to produce a single 768-dimension vector per participant.

Pooled machine learning model.

First we established whether MentalRoBERTa embeddings extracted from participants' open-ended responses could predict baseline internalizing symptoms across the full sample. We trained a ridge regression model 78 on the full sample (N = 1,685) using the textTrainRegression function from the Text package in R 55 with cross-validation (5 outer folds). In each outer fold, 20% of data was held out as a test set; the remaining 80% was split into a training set (75%) and a validation set (25%) for penalty selection. Ridge penalties (λ) ranging from 10⁻⁸ to 10⁸ were optimized via grid search minimizing RMSE on the validation set, with all splits stratified by outcome quartile. We report one-tailed Pearson correlations between predicted and observed scores as our primary performance metric.

Group-specific machine learning models.

We then asked whether language-based prediction differed across racial/ethnic groups by training ridge regression models separately within each group. Because each group's sample size fell below the number of embedding dimensions (N White = 412, N Black = 522, N Asian = 369, N Latino/Hispanic = 382; N parameters = 768), regularization must scale proportionally to the ratio of embedding dimensions to sample size 78 . We therefore fixed the regularization penalty at λ = 250 for all group models. Fixing λ uniformly across groups also enables direct comparison of the resulting coefficient vectors (β), as differences in β cannot be attributed to differences in regularization, an approach consistent with prior race-stratified language modeling work 29.

Cross-group generalization.

To test how well each group's model generalized when applied across-group to every other group, we computed a cross-group error difference for each participant. This can be expressed as: dᵢ = |across-group errorᵢ| -|within-group errorᵢ|, where across-group errorᵢ is the error produced by the outside (applied) model on participant i, and in-group errorᵢ is the error produced by participant i's own group's dedicated model on that same participant. Positive values indicate that a group's internalizing symptoms were predicted less accurately by a model trained on another group's data compared to its own group's model. Negative values indicate the reverse. We tested whether mean cross-group error differences differed from zero across the 12 model-group pairings using paired t-tests, with p-values FDR-corrected and confidence intervals constructed via bootstrapping (5,000 iterations with replacement). We applied an identical procedure to test prospective generalization, training group-specific ridge regression models on Session 1 (baseline) language to predict Session 2 (follow-up) internalizing symptoms collected three weeks later (see Table S14 for results). To test whether language predicted follow-up symptoms beyond baseline severity, we additionally compared models including both baseline symptoms and language to see if they predicted follow-up symptoms beyond models including baseline symptoms alone (see Supplemental Information).

What do these machine learning models learn differently for each race? Since a ridge regression model trained on embeddings learns a 768-dimensional coefficient vector (β) (i.e., a line of best fit) pointing from low-to high-severity language in embedding space, a participant's predicted severity score is simply their response's projection onto this vector. This geometric structure affords a form of interpretability through projecting individual word embeddings onto the vector, by taking the dot product, allowing us to recover each word's contribution to severity predictions 43 . One can then construct a difference vector that represents differences in how words are weighted by each model simply by subtracting vectors for one ridge regression from the other 79 . Projecting words onto this difference vector then identifies words that are weighted differently across groups, revealing what each model has learned to treat as a marker of distress. We exploited this property to characterize which words each group's model differentially weighted as indicators of symptom severity, revealing the extent to which racial/ethnic groups rely on distinct linguistic signals when expressing psychological distress, and whether systematic differences in these signals might relate to differences in cross-group prediction error. Difference vectors were constructed by subtracting one group's L2-normalized β vector from another group's and renormalizing this difference vector (e.g., (β White -β Black ) / ||β White -β Black ||), so that positive projection scores indicate stronger association with severity in the first group's model and negative scores indicate the reverse. We found that the White group's vector was the most geometrically distinctive of the four (mean pairwise cosine similarity to other groups' β vectors: 0.807, which is less than other racial groups' average similarity from each other: 0.847; Table S13). Thus, we constructed a summary contrast by subtracting the mean of the three minority β vectors from the White vector and renormalizing. This yielded a single axis capturing the aggregate direction in which the White model's learned severity signal diverges from those of the minority group models. We additionally computed difference vectors for each individual pairwise comparison (e.g., White vs. Black, White vs. Asian, White vs. Latino/Hispanic); these are reported in the Supplemental Information (Figure S2) and showed patterns broadly consistent with the aggregate contrast reported here.

We compiled a list of all words used across participants, excluding common stopwords and words occurring less than 50 times, while retaining first-person pronouns throughout. Morphological variants were collapsed via stemming with the most frequent surface form retained (e.g., "happier_", "happy;", "happiest"), embeddings were averaged to yield a single embedding per word type 55 . For each pairwise comparison, we used the union of both groups' word lists, averaging embeddings for words used by both groups. We mean-centered word embeddings using the frequency-weighted corpus mean, so that projection scores reflect what is semantically distinctive about each word rather than its absolute position in embedding space. We then projected each word onto the pairwise difference vectors described above, yielding a score that reflects how differently the two groups' models weight that word as a marker of symptom severity.

Because both our language variables and our outcome variable are related to symptom severity, this raised the possibility that the observed race-language interactions could partly reflect between-group differences in baseline severity rather than differences in the relationship between language and symptoms.

We used entropy balancing 39 to address this concern via the WeightIt R package 40 . Briefly, entropy balancing is a reweighting procedure that assigns each participant a weight such that a specified covariate distribution is exactly equated across groups, while minimizing the exclusion of any participants. This distinguishes it from other types of matching-based approaches (e.g., propensity score or nearest-neighbor matching), which achieve covariate balance by selectively excluding unmatched cases but can substantially reduce statistical power, particularly for smaller groups. Among the (infinite) set of possible weights that would achieve exact balance on the target covariate, entropy balancing selects the set that remains maximally close to uniform weighting (i.e., minimizes the entropy distance from a weight of 1 for every participant), which prevents the reweighted estimates from being driven disproportionately by a small number of extreme-weighted individuals.

We specified that the model should balance all four racial/ethnic groups to the pooled mean of baseline internalizing severity across the sample. This produced exact mean balance across groups (standardized mean difference = 0; weighted M = 12.82 for all groups) and near-exact variance balance (variance ratio = 1.12). Weights ranged from 2.84 to 5.15 (M = 4.00), and effective sample sizes were retained at 98.0-99.9% of the unweighted N in every group (White: 411/412; Black: 514/522; Asian: 369/369; Latino/Hispanic: 375/382).

We then reran our primary race/ethnicity-language interaction models predicting internalizing severity from the interaction of race/ethnicity and each of the LIWC language variables (I-usage, positive tone, and negative tone) with significant interactions, covarying age, sex, and education on the entropy-balanced sample. We used weighted regression with bootstrapped standard errors (R = 5,000 replications) to account for the additional estimation uncertainty introduced by the weights themselves. Because bootstrapped/sandwich variance-covariance matrices do not support a classical F-test with well-defined denominator degrees of freedom, omnibus interaction tests are reported as Wald χ² statistics.

All three race/ethnicity-language interactions remained significant following severity balancing and FDR correction: I-usage, χ²(3) = 9.89, p FDR = .029; negative tone, χ²(3) = 8.31, p FDR = .040; positive tone, χ²(3) = 10.18, p FDR = .029. We additionally examined FDR-corrected pairwise contrasts for each interaction to identify which specific group comparisons were driving each omnibus effect (Table S4). The I-usage interaction retained individually significant pairwise contrasts as reported in the full sample: White participants' I-usage slope differed significantly from both Black (p FDR = .032) and Latino/Hispanic (p FDR = .032) participants' slopes, closely replicating the pattern observed in the unweighted analysis. Neither tone variable retained significant pairwise contrasts after correction (all ps > .11; Table S4), but the omnibus interaction remained significant and the direction of differences were the same: For negative tone, the Latino/Hispanic slope was stronger than all others, and for positive tone, the Asian slope was stronger than all others (See Table S3).

Exploratory LIWC Variables

We Words. We-word usage did not significantly predict internalizing symptoms in any group, and there was no significant interaction between We-word use and race/ethnicity (F(3, 1662) = 1.32, p = .267). Slopes for each group were small and directionally inconsistent (see Tables S7-S8; See Figure S1a). We-word usage thus does not appear to be a reliable marker of internalizing distress in this sample, regardless of racial/ethnic group.

Social Words.

Social word usage did not significantly predict internalizing symptoms in any group, and there was no significant interaction between social word use and race/ethnicity (F(3, 1662) = 1.40, p = .243). Slopes for each group were small and directionally inconsistent (see Tables S7-S8; see Figure S1b). Social word usage thus does not appear to be a reliable marker of internalizing distress in this sample, regardless of racial/ethnic group.

Cognitive Processing Words.

The Cognitive Processing × race/ethnicity interaction term was not significant (F(3, 1662) = 0.22, p = .886), indicating no reliable evidence that the association between cognitive processing word usage and internalizing symptoms differs by race/ethnicity. Nonetheless, in post-hoc group-level tests, the confidence interval for Black participants excluded zero, though this effect did not survive FDR correction (p FDR = .188; see Table S7; see Figure S1c). No other group showed evidence of an effect with slopes that were positive and similar in magnitude across all four groups. Given the null omnibus interaction and the failure of the Black group effect to survive correction, cognitive processing word usage does not appear to be a reliable marker of internalizing distress in this sample, and there is no evidence that its relationship with symptoms varies by race/ethnicity.

Coefficient Vector Similarity

To complement the machine learning analyses reported in the main text, we examined pairwise cosine similarities between the group-specific model coefficient vectors. This provided us with a direct measure of how similarly each racial/ethnic group's model weights language features (in this case word embeddings) when predicting symptoms.

Figure S2. Contrast Vector Visualization. Each panel shows one pairwise comparison between two race/ethnicity groups' learned β vectors, labeled by panel title (e.g., "White vs. Black"). Within a panel, a word's position reflects how differently the two named groups' models associate that word with internalizing symptom severity: positive values indicate the first-named group's model links the word more strongly to high severity than the second-named group's model does; negative values indicate the reverse. Bar color identifies which of the two groups' models weights the word more heavily toward severity, following the four-group color scheme used throughout (White, Black, Asian, Latino/Hispanic). The x-axis reflects how much more strongly one model weights that word toward severity than the other, with larger absolute values indicating greater disagreement in how strongly the word signals severity. Panels show the top and bottom 15 words drawn from the union vocabulary of the two compared groups (minimum word frequency = 50). All group-specific models were fitted with matched hyperparameters (fixed λ = 250) so that differences reflect group differences in language rather than differences in model regularization.

Prospective Prediction

Having established that language-based markers of internalizing severity differ across racial/ethnic groups at baseline, we next asked whether these differences have prospective implications. That is, whether the same baseline language features that track concurrent symptom severity also predict symptom levels three weeks later, and whether that predictive signal varies by race/ethnicity.

Participants and Attrition.

Of the 1,685 participants who completed baseline measures, 1,465 (86.9%) completed the follow-up survey approximately three weeks later, yielding an attrition rate of 13.1% (N = 220). Retention rates differed significantly across racial/ethnic groups (χ²(3) = 15.60, p = .001): White participants had the highest retention (92.0%), followed by Black (87.4%), Asian (84.3%), and Latino/Hispanic (83.5%) participants. To characterize differential attrition, we estimated a single logistic regression model predicting follow-up completion from baseline internalizing severity, race/ethnicity, age, sex, and education level. Neither baseline internalizing severity (OR = 0.99, 95% CI [0.98, 1.00], p = .14), age (OR = 1.07, 95% CI [0.92, 1.25], p = .364), sex (all p > .13), nor education level (all p > .12) significantly predicted follow-up completion, indicating that attrition was unrelated to symptom severity or these demographic factors. FDR-corrected pairwise contrasts on race/ethnicity indicated that White participants were significantly more likely to complete Session 2 than Asian (OR = 2.07, 95% CI [1.10, 3.89], p = .007) and Latino/Hispanic participants (OR = 2.20, 95% CI [1.19, 4.07], p = .004); the White-Black contrast did not survive correction (OR = 1.62, 95% CI [0.89, 2.94], p = .068). No other pairwise group differences were significant (all p FDR > .17). All primary analyses are reported for the full baseline sample (N = 1,685); follow-up analyses presented in the supplement are based on the 1,465 participants with complete longitudinal data.

LIWC Prediction of Follow-Up Symptoms.

We re-estimated each moderation model with follow-up internalizing symptoms as the outcome, controlling for baseline symptoms and demographics, to isolate the prospective signal in language beyond symptom stability. Repeating these analyses on follow-up data showed that no LIWC language feature showed a significant race moderation when controlling for baseline symptoms: I-usage (F(3, 1441) = 0.26, p = .856), negative tone (F(3, 1441) = 0.89, p = .444), positive tone (F(3, 1441) = 0.69, p = .557), we-words (F(3, 1441) = 0.58, p = .630), social words (F(3, 1441) = 0.53, p = .661), and cognitive processing words (F(3, 1441) = 1.75, p = .155). Importantly, we in fact observed that group-level slopes were uniformly small and none survived FDR correction (p FDR > .05).

These null results indicate that (i) LIWC language features captured at Session 1 (baseline) do not predict follow-up ratings after controlling for baseline symptoms, and (ii) no LIWC language features differentially predict symptom change depending on one's racial/ethnic group. We conducted a series of follow-up tests to investigate why we found no prospective symptom prediction using LIWC variables. These analyses showed that internalizing symptoms were highly stable across the 3-week interval between sessions. Session 1 and Session 2 scores were very strongly correlated (r = .817, 95% CI [.799, .833], p < .001), indicating that individual differences in symptom severity were largely preserved over time. Machine Learning Models Predicting Follow-Up Symptoms While Controlling For Baseline Symptoms.

The models above provide evidence that language shows differential prediction of symptoms beyond the current timepoint, but because they do not control for baseline symptoms (as the LIWC analyses did), they do not show that language can predict changes in symptoms beyond baseline levels. Following recent recommendations for evaluating prospective prediction 80 , we next tested whether language improved prediction beyond what baseline symptoms alone could achieve. We first performed this comparison in the pooled sample of all participants who completed follow-up (N = 1,465), comparing a model that predicted follow-up symptoms from baseline symptoms alone to one that used both baseline symptoms and participants' language. As with the other pooled models, the penalty was selected through cross-validation, so we fit this model with the text package, entering baseline symptoms as an additional predictor alongside the language embeddings. We then performed the same comparison within each group. Both models were tested on the same cross-validation splits. In the combined group-specific models, language was regularized with the same fixed penalty used throughout the paper (λ = 250), but baseline symptoms were left unpenalized so the model could use them in full. Because the text package does not allow a single predictor to go unpenalized, we fit these group-specific models with glmnett 81 . We then tested whether adding language reduced prediction error (paired t-tests on each participant's absolute error) and how much it changed accuracy (the difference in correlations, Δr, with 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals). P-values for the group-specific models were corrected for multiple comparisons across the four groups.

Adding language did not improve prediction of follow-up symptoms beyond baseline symptoms (Table S15). In the pooled sample, adding language to baseline symptoms slightly reduced accuracy (r = .761 vs. .816; Δr = -.055, 95% CI [-.069, -.041]; t(1464) = -10.9, p < .001). Within groups, combined models (i.e., baseline symptoms and language) performed nearly identically to baseline-only models: White (r = .766 vs. .760; Δr = .005, 95% CI [-.004, .015], p FDR = .66), Black (r = .824 vs. .823; Δr = .001, 95% CI [-.003, .006], p FDR = .99), Latino/Hispanic (r = .825 vs. .827; Δr = -.002, 95% CI [-.009, .005], p FDR = .66), and Asian (r = .845 vs. .846; Δr = -.001, 95% CI [-.006, .003], p FDR = .99). We also tested whether the prospective cross-group differences reported above reflected language once baseline symptoms were controlled. For each of the 12 model-group pairings, we computed the cross-group error differential (dᵢ) for the combined models and subtracted the same quantity from the baseline-only models, isolating the portion attributable to language. None were significant (all p FDR ≥ .85; Table S16).

Together, these results indicate that the prospective predictions reported above do not survive when baseline symptom severity is controlled for. Group differences in the accuracy of language-based estimates persist to symptom reports three weeks later, but language did not predict change in symptoms beyond baseline, for any group.

Author notes: *Correspondence should be addressed to Steven Mesquiti (email: sm9518@princeton.edu) This file includes: Supplementary text Figs. S1 to S3 Tables S1 to S16 Measurement Invariance Prior to primary analyses, we tested measurement invariance of the PHQ-8 and GAD-7 across racial/ethnic groups using multi-group confirmatory factor analysis (MGCFA). We specified a unidimensional factor structure for each scale and estimated three progressively constrained models: configural invariance (same factor structure across groups, all parameters freely estimated), metric invariance (factor loadings additionally constrained to equality across groups), and scalar invariance (item thresholds additionally constrained to equality across groups). All models were estimated using the diagonally weighted least squares (DWLS) estimator with ordered categorical indicators, appropriate for ordinal Likert-type items. Invariance was evaluated using changes in CFI and RMSEA between nested models 72 . White participants served as the reference group throughout.

Both scales demonstrated full scalar invariance across all four racial/ethnic groups. For the PHQ-8, CFI remained stable across metric (CFI = .998, ΔCFI = .0001) and scalar (CFI = .998, ΔCFI = .0003) constraints, with RMSEA improving monotonically from configural to scalar (.063 → .058 → .048), indicating that the successive equality constraints stabilized rather than degraded model fit. For the GAD-7, fit indices were similarly stable across metric (CFI = .999, ΔCFI = .0001) and scalar (CFI = .999, ΔCFI = .0004) constraints, with RMSEA again improving from configural to scalar (.063 → .060 → .041). Taken together, these results affirm that the PHQ-8 and GAD-7 measure their respective constructs equivalently across racial/ethnic groups at the scale level, supporting the validity of group mean comparisons.

Full scalar invariance criteria: ΔCFI < .010, ΔRMSEA < .015. All ΔCFI values < .001; unrounded values are .0001 (PHQ-8 and GAD-7 metric), .0003 (PHQ-8 scalar), and .0004 (GAD-7 scalar).

Robustness Check Group differences in internalizing symptoms. To test whether our racial/ethnic groups differed in symptom severity, we conducted a one-way ANOVA. We observed that racial/ethnic groups in our sample differed in mean baseline internalizing severity (PHQ-8 + GAD-7 composite; White M = 13.2, SD = 11.5; Black M = 11.4, SD = 11.4; Asian M = 12.6, SD = 11.7; Latino/Hispanic M = 14.5, SD = 12.65, F(3, 1681) = 5.52, p < .001). Tukey HSD-adjusted pairwise comparisons revealed that this effect was driven primarily by Latino/Hispanic participants, who reported significantly higher internalizing symptoms than Black participants (p < .001). No other pairwise comparisons reached significance (all p's > .07; see Table S2), including the Latino/Hispanic-Asian contrast, which showed a similar-sized gap but did not survive correction.

Table S2. Internalizing Symptom Pairwise Comparisons Across Race/Ethnicity point on average (M CHANGE = 0.82, SD CHANGE = 6.93, M PRE = 12.64, SD PRE = 11.76; M FU = 11.83, SD FU = 11.05). Taken together, these results indicate that internalizing symptoms remained largely stable across the 3-week interval, leaving comparatively little within-person variance for Session-1 language features to predict at follow-up.

Machine Learning Models Predicting Follow-Up Symptoms Without Controlling For Baseline Symptoms.

To test whether Session 1 (baseline) language predicted follow-up internalizing symptoms 3 weeks later, we estimated a parallel set of ridge regression models using the same architecture and hyperparameters described above. A pooled prospective model was trained on the follow-up sample (N = 1,465) using 5-fold cross-validation with penalty selection via grid search (as described for the baseline models); group-specific prospective models used the fixed penalty of λ = 250. All prospective models used Session 1 language embeddings as predictors and Session 2 internalizing symptoms as the outcome, with no baseline symptom covariate included in the machine learning models themselves (models controlling for baseline symptoms are reported below).

The pooled model demonstrated moderate accuracy predicting follow-up symptoms from baseline language (r = 0.565, 95%CI [0.535, 1], p < .001). Within-group models showed comparable prospective validity across groups: White (r = 0.470, 95%CI [0.401, 1]), Black (r = 0.506, 95%CI [0.447, 1]), Latino/Hispanic (r = 0.619, 95%CI [0.559, 1]), and Asian (r = 0.594, 95%CI [0.530, 1]; all p's < .001). A one-way ANOVA revealed no significant differences in absolute prediction errors across racial/ethnic groups (F(3, 1461) = 1.775, p = .150) indicating comparable prospective model performance across groups.

Without controlling for baseline symptoms, cross-group generalization revealed a pattern mirroring the findings for concurrent models. The White-trained model again produced significantly higher across-group error when applied to Latino/Hispanic (p FDR = .001), Asian (p FDR < .001), and Black participants (p FDR = .029) (see Table S14 for full statistics). Again, the Black-trained model generalized significantly poorly to Asian participants (p FDR = .027), and the Asian-trained model produced significantly lower across-group error on White participants (p FDR = .029). As for the baseline model, across all 12 pairings, the White model remained the only model to produce significantly higher errors on all three out-group comparisons (see Figure S3; see Table S14).

Values reflect the mean difference between the two (dᵢ[baseline + language] -dᵢ[baseline only]), which isolates the portion of cross-group prediction error attributable to language.
